titleEn: Book of the Dead of Ani — Spells 29, 27, 58 and 59
part: Spells 29, 27, 58 and 59 — keeping the heart; breath and water in the necropolis (Plates 15–16)
about: Four short spells on Plates 15 and 16 of Ani's papyrus, written after Spells 61 and 54. In Spells 29 and 27 Ani keeps his heart: he turns back a messenger of the gods who has come for it, and he tells the takers of hearts that his heart is his own and obeys him. In Spells 58 and 59 he asks for breath and water in the necropolis: he answers the keepers of a door, names the parts of his boat, and begs water and air from the sycamore of the sky-goddess Nut. Budge prints three chapters from other papyri between Spells 27 and 58, which are left out; many words here are rare or doubtful, and the notes say so.

sentences.l: spell · of · not · letting · be-taken-away · the-heart · of · a-man · from-him · in · the-necropolis
sentences.i: Spell for not letting the heart of a man be taken away from him in the necropolis.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes ḥm·tw; read nḥm·tw. The bowl ḥm (coded N41, approximate) with m as complement, t and the chick w are printed, but not the water n with which nḥm 'take away' begins; the same title in Spell 61 has it, and the sense allows no other word. Spell 29 begins. The papyrus writes rꜣ n tmt rdit ḥm·tw in red, then ib n s in black, m-ꜥ·f in red again, and m ẖrt-nṯr in black. ·tw makes the passive sḏm·tw·f after rdi, 'letting (the heart) be taken away'. rꜣ n 'spell for' is the mouth with its stroke and water n, as in every title. tmt is t, the sledge tm (U15) and the owl m as complement, with a second t after them: the negative verb tm 'not to do', as in Spell 61, where the second t is not written (Budge also reads temt). rdit is the mouth r, t and the arm (D36, no loaf): the negatival complement, 'not letting'. ib 'heart' is the heart with its stroke, and ib n s 'the heart of a man' is the genitive written with n; s is the bolt, a stroke and the seated man. m-ꜥ·f 'from him' is the compound preposition m-ꜥ, here the owl m with the arm ꜥ drawn across it in one ligature, and the viper ·f. m 'in' is the sign m (Aa15), and ẖrt-nṯr 'the necropolis' is the flag nṯr, written first out of respect, the loop r (coded D21, approximate) and the block ẖr (T28), as in Spell 61. The heart (ib) was the seat of mind and memory: without it the dead man could neither think nor answer at the judgement.

sentences.l: said · by · the-Osiris · Ani · true-of-voice · behind-you · messenger · of · god · every
sentences.i: Said by the Osiris Ani, true of voice: Back, you messenger of every god!
sentences.n: The papyrus writes ḏd in in red. ḏd in N 'said by N', as before: the cobra and the hand in one ligature, then in, written here with the sign in (coded W25, approximate) and water n as complement. wsir is the low seat (coded Q2, approximate) over the eye, ꜣny has the squatting man with a flail (A52), and mꜣꜥ-ḫrw 'true of voice' is the plinth mꜣꜥ and the oar ḫrw, without the sickle. ḥꜣ·k is the papyrus clump ḥꜣ (M16) with ꜣ as complement, a small head (coded D1, approximate) as classifier, and ·k: the preposition ḥꜣ 'behind' with a suffix, 'behind you!', the cry that turns something back, as in Spell 17. wpwty 'messenger' is the horns wp (coded F13, approximate) with p as complement, t, the chick w and two strokes y; the t is written before the w (Budge: àptui). Budge prints a small × high above the walking legs at the end; it is taken as the crossed sticks (Z9), the classifier of crossing that wpwtyw has in the Address of Spell 125, and the legs as the classifier of going. The × may instead be a printer's mark. n nṯr nb 'of every god': water n, the flag with the seated god, and the basket nb, 'every' after its noun. The messengers of the gods were sent to fetch and to punish; this one has come for Ani's heart.

sentences.l: (in) · (iw) · have-come-you · for · heart-my · this · of · the-living
sentences.i: Have you come for this heart of mine, which belongs to the living?
sentences.n: in, the reed and water n, and iw, the reed and the chick, open the sentence together: in iw marks a question, 'is it that …?' (Budge: àn àu, 'is it that'). Neither is translated on its own. ii·n·k 'you have come' is the reed with legs (M18), which writes ii 'come', the reed i as complement, the walking legs (printed as a small Λ), water n and the basket ·k: the sḏm·n·f. r 'for' is the mouth. ḥꜣty·i 'my heart' is the forepart of a lion ḥꜣt with t as complement, two strokes y, the heart as classifier and the seated man ·i, as in Spell 26; the second word for heart, beside ib. pn 'this' (p and n) follows the suffix, as it must. n ꜥnḫw is the genitive n with ꜥnḫw 'the living', the sign ꜥnḫ (S34) with n and ḫ as complements, the chick w and a stroke. Budge takes it as 'which liveth'; the genitive with the plural noun gives 'of the living', a heart that belongs among the living. The next line writes the same word with the seated man, the classifier of people, which supports that reading. Ani speaks to the messenger.

sentences.l: not · shall-be-given · to-you · heart-my · this · of · the-living
sentences.i: This heart of mine, which belongs to the living, shall not be given to you.
sentences.n: nn is the negative arms (coded D35, approximate) with water n: with the sḏm·f, 'shall not', the negative of the future. Budge prints ṭātu-nek as one group; it is split here into di·tw and n·k (q re-indexed). di·tw is the giving hand with its loaf (D37), the form of rdi without its r, then t and the chick w: the passive sḏm·tw·f, '(shall not) be given'. n·k 'to you' is water n and ·k. ḥꜣty·i pn n ꜥnḫw as in the line before; here ꜥnḫw has the seated man and a stroke as classifiers, the sign of people. The question was a challenge, and this is the refusal: the heart stays with its owner.

sentences.l: striding(?) · hear · the-gods · the-offerings · to-me · (ḥr) · fall-they · on · faces-their · all(?) · to · the-ground · themselves
sentences.i: Striding(?), the gods hear the offerings made to me, and they fall on their faces, all of them(?), to the ground of their own accord.
sentences.n: The passage is obscure, and the rendering follows the order of the signs. ḫndw is ḫ and water n, then the mountain (coded N26, approximate), which writes ḏw, standing here for d, then the chick w and the walking legs (a small Λ): taken as ḫnd 'tread, stride', the w being the plural ending of a participle, not a complement of the mountain (Budge: χenṭu, 'advancing'). Who strides is not said. sḏm 'hear' is the ear (F21) with m as complement, and nṯrw 'the gods', the flag three times, is its noun subject: the sḏm·f, 'the gods hear'. ḥtpt 'offerings' is the offering-mat ḥtp (R4) with t and p as complements and t. Budge prints the mouth r and the seated man as two groups and marks the r (sic); they are joined here as r·i 'to me' (q re-indexed). If the r is a slip, the phrase is ḥtpt·i 'my offerings'; the reading keeps what stands. ḥr, the face with its stroke, has no English in Budge. It is taken as the preposition ḥr with the infinitive ḫr 'fall', whose subject is the suffix: 'and they fall', what follows on the hearing. ḫr·sn is ḫ and r with a falling man (coded A15, approximate) as classifier, and ·sn (the bolt, water n and plural strokes). ḥr ḥr·sn 'on their faces': the preposition, then the noun 'face' with ·sn, both the face with its stroke. The next group is the bolt, t and water n, then the owl m, and t over plural strokes; Budge marks it (sic) twice and reads temt, 'all of them'. The bolt and the water n are not explained. It is taken with him as tmt 'all', from tm 'be complete', but the reading is doubtful. m tꜣ 'to the ground' is the owl and the strip of land with grains (coded N16, approximate). ḏs·sn is the cobra ḏ and the bolt s with plural strokes, and ·sn: ḏs 'self', 'of their own accord'. The gods bow to the ground before one who receives offerings: the speaker claims the rank of a god. Spell 29 ends here.

sentences.l: spell · of · not · letting · be-taken · the-heart · of · a-man · from-him · in · the-necropolis
sentences.i: Spell for not letting the heart of a man be taken from him in the necropolis.
sentences.n: Spell 27 begins, and Budge's line numerals start again at 1. The papyrus writes rꜣ n tmt rdit iṯ in red, ḥꜣty n s in black, m-ꜥ·f in red, and m ẖrt-nṯr in black. rꜣ n tmt rdit as in Spell 29. iṯ 'take' is the tether ṯ with the walking legs under it, the one sign that writes iṯ (V15; coded here as the tether V13, approximate, and the legs), then t, written for ṯ as a complement, and the low hooked sign (U15), the sign printed for the arm with a stick, the classifier of force (Budge: θet). No reed i and no tw are written. It is taken as the passive sḏm·f after rdi, 'letting (the heart) be taken', as the nḥm·tw of Spell 29 asks; 'letting (anyone) take' is also possible. ḥꜣty 'heart' is the forepart of a lion ḥꜣt with t, two strokes y and the heart as classifier: the second word for heart. s, m-ꜥ·f, m (the owl here) and ẖrt-nṯr as in Spell 29. The two heart spells stand side by side on the papyrus, one after the other.

sentences.l: said · by · the-Osiris · Ani · O · takers · of-hearts · (nqfywt)
sentences.i: Said by the Osiris Ani: O you who take away hearts, (nqfywt?)!
sentences.n: The papyrus writes ḏd in in red; the name is black. ḏd in wsir ꜣny as in Spell 29: Budge prints no transliteration under the cobra and hand, but they are the same ligature. ꜣny has the squatting man with a flail. i 'O' is the reed with the man with hand to mouth (A2), the gesture of calling. iṯyw is iṯ 'take', written as in the title, with two reeds y and a stroke: the plural participle, 'those who take', its w not written (Budge: θeti, 'takers away'). ibw 'hearts' is the heart with two strokes, the second tall and dashed, for the plural, and iṯyw ibw is the direct genitive, 'takers of hearts'. The next word, which Budge prints at the head of Plate 16, is water n, the hill-slope q (N29), the viper f, two reeds y, the chick w, t, the low hooked sign (U15) and a stroke. It is not known. Budge reads neqefiut and renders '[hail] stealers [of hearts]', supplying the bracketed words. The low sign may be the classifier of force, which would suit a verb of seizing or striking, but that is a guess, and the word is left untranslated. The takers of hearts are demons who rob the dead of the heart, and with it of mind and memory.

sentences.i: It is done(?) for you.
sentences.n: irt is the eye ir with t, and n·tn is water n with t, water n and plural strokes. Budge prints en and ten as two groups and renders the three 'Ye have done'; n and tn are joined here as n·tn 'for you' (q re-indexed), plural, the takers of hearts. irt is taken as the passive participle of iri 'do', feminine as a neuter, 'what is done', and the clause as a sentence without a verb: '(it is) done for you'. Read as the sḏm·n·f, 'you have done' (Budge), the t would be unexplained; read as one word, the relative form irt·n·tn 'what you have done', feminine as a neuter, it is explained, as in irt·n·f in line 4, and that reading is as possible. How these words join what comes before and after is not clear, and the sense is doubtful.

sentences.i: Hail to you, lords of eternity, who hold(?) everlastingness!
sentences.n: ind-ḥr·tn is the reed i and the sign nḏ (coded Aa27, approximate) with ḏ as complement and the roll, then the face ḥr with its stroke and ·tn: ind ḥr·tn, 'greetings to your face, hail to you', the greeting of Spell 147, said here to several. nbw 'lords' is the basket nb with the chick w and a stroke. ḥḥ is the wick ḥ, the sun and a second ḥ: nḥḥ 'eternity', its n not written, as in the hymn to Osiris and in Spell 1. ẖryw is the block ẖr (T28) with r, two reeds y and a small bird (coded G37, approximate) over plural strokes: the plural nisba of ẖr 'under', 'those who are under'. ẖr also means 'carrying, in the keeping of', and the word is taken as 'who hold' (Budge: χeri, 'possessors of'). The small bird is the classifier of small and bad things, and it is not explained here. ḏt 'everlastingness' is the cobra ḏ and t with the land sign (coded N16, approximate). nḥḥ and ḏt are the two words for eternity, time that returns and time that stays. Whether the lords of eternity are the takers of hearts under a politer name, or other beings, is not said.

sentences.l: do-not · take · heart · this · of · the-Osiris · Ani · with · fingers-your · (nor) · heart-his · this · there
sentences.i: Do not take this heart (ib) of the Osiris Ani with your fingers, nor this heart (ḥꜣty) of his, there.
sentences.n: m 'do not!' is the owl: the negative imperative. iṯ 'take' is written as in the title: the negatival complement after m. ib pn n wsir ꜣny 'this heart of the Osiris Ani'; here ꜣny has the seated man (A1) as classifier. Budge's line 3 begins with m ḏbꜥw·tn 'with your fingers', the owl (m of the instrument) and three fingers (D50) for the plural ḏbꜥw, with ·tn. ḥꜣty·f is the forepart of a lion, t, two strokes, the heart and ·f, then pn 'this' and im 'there', the reed and the owl. ḥꜣty·f pn im stands without a verb and is taken as a second object of the same order: '(nor) this heart of his there', the ḥꜣty beside the ib, as in Spell 26. English has one word for the two hearts, and the Egyptian word is given in brackets. The fingers are the hands of the demons that snatch.

sentences.i: You shall not bring evil words into being against it.
sentences.n: nn 'not' is written here with water n twice: with the sḏm·f, 'shall not'. sḫprw·tn is the bolt s, the causative prefix, the scarab ḫpr with r as complement, the chick w and a stroke, and ·tn: sḫpr 'bring into being, cause to happen', the causative of ḫpr, in the prospective sḏm·f, its w the ending. ḏdt 'words' is the fire-drill (coded U28, approximate), standing for ḏ, the hand d, t, the man with hand to mouth and a stroke: the noun from ḏd 'say'. ḏwt 'evil' is the mountain ḏw (coded N26, approximate) with t and w, the small bird of bad things (coded G37, approximate) and plural strokes; it follows ḏdt as an adjective, feminine to agree. r·f 'against it', r and ·f, is the heart. Words spoken against the heart before the gods could condemn its owner.

sentences.l: because · belongs · heart · this · to · the-Osiris · Ani · (n) · heart · this · of · the-great · of-names · the-mighty-one
sentences.i: For this heart belongs to the Osiris Ani: this heart is that of the one great of names, the mighty one.
sentences.n: ḥr-ntt 'because' is the face ḥr with its stroke, water n and t twice: the compound conjunction, as in the Address. iry is the reed, r and two strokes y: the nisba of r 'to', 'belonging to', here the predicate, with ib pn as its subject and n 'to' before the owner, 'this heart belongs to the Osiris Ani'. ꜣny has the seated man (A1). A water n follows that has no English in Budge and adds nothing clear; it is not translated, and it may repeat the n before wsir. ib pn n ꜥꜣ rnw is a sentence without a verb, 'this heart is of the one great of names'. ꜥꜣ is the column ꜥꜣ (coded O29, approximate) with the arm ꜥ as complement and the roll (Y1). rnw 'names' is the mouth r, water n, the pot nw (W24) and the chick w for the plural ending, and the man with hand to mouth with a stroke. ꜥꜣ rnw, an adjective followed by the noun that says in what respect, is 'great of names'. wr 'the mighty one' is the swallow wr (coded G36, approximate) with r. Many names marked a great god, and the heart is claimed for such a god.

sentences.l: words-his · (are)-for · limbs-his · sends(?)-he · heart-his · which-is-foremost-in · body-his
sentences.i: His words are for his limbs; he sends(?) his heart, which is foremost in his body.
sentences.n: ḏdt·f 'his words' is written as ḏdt in line 3, with ·f. n is water n: the preposition 'to, for', in a sentence without a verb, 'his words are for his limbs', perhaps that his limbs do what he says. Budge renders it 'in', reading n for m, as later writing often has; that is possible too. ꜥt·f is the arm ꜥ, t, a small piece of flesh (coded F51, approximate) as classifier, a stroke and ·f: ꜥt 'limb, member', used of the limbs together. hb·f is the courtyard h (O4), the foot b, the walking legs (a small Λ) and ·f. It is taken as hꜣb 'send', its ꜣ not written, with ib·f as its object, 'he sends his heart' (Budge: heb-f, 'goeth forth'); the reading is uncertain. ḫnty is the rack of jars ḫnt (coded W17, approximate) with n and t as complements and two strokes y: the nisba 'foremost, who is at the head of', after the noun it describes. Budge's line 4 begins with ẖt·f 'his body', the belly ẖ (F32) with t, a stroke and ·f. The heart was thought to rule the body: it plans, and the limbs carry out what it says.

sentences.i: His heart is pleasing(?) to the gods.
sentences.n: The first group is the sickle mꜣ (U1) laid across the vulture ꜣ in one ligature, t, the heart and the man with hand to mouth. Budge reads mat, 'pleasant'. No word mꜣt with the heart as classifier is met elsewhere in these parts, and both reading and sense are uncertain. It is taken as an adjective-verb that stands first in the sentence, with ib·f as its subject, 'pleasing is his heart', the heart sign classifying a word of feeling. ib·f 'his heart', r 'to' and nṯrw 'the gods', the flag three times.

sentences.l: the-heart · of · the-Osiris · Ani · true-of-voice · to-him · has-power-he · over-it
sentences.i: The heart of the Osiris Ani, true of voice, is his; he has power over it.
sentences.n: ib n wsir ꜣny 'the heart of the Osiris Ani', and mꜣꜥ-ḫrw, the plinth and the oar. Budge prints maāχeru-nef as one group, 'victorious is he'. It is split here into mꜣꜥ-ḫrw, the usual epithet, and n·f, water n with ·f (q re-indexed). n·f 'to him' is the predicate of a sentence without a verb, with ib n wsir ꜣny as its subject: 'the heart of the Osiris Ani is his', as ib·i n·i 'my heart is mine' in Spell 26. sḫm·f 'he has power' is the sceptre sḫm (coded S42, approximate) with m as complement, written with the owl-and-arm ligature, and ·f. The arm is not read: it stands where sḫm has the classifier of force, as in sḫm·i in Spell 26 (Budge: seχem-f). sḫm m is 'have power over', and im·f, the reed and the owl with ·f, is m before a suffix, 'over it', the heart.

sentences.i: It shall not tell what he has done.
sentences.n: nn as in Spell 29 (the arms D35 and water n), with the sḏm·f ḏd·f, the cobra and hand with ·f: 'it shall not say'. irt·n·f is the eye ir, t, water n and ·f: the relative form sḏm·n·f of iri, feminine as a neuter, 'what he has done' (Budge prints àrit-nef as one group, '[what] hath been done to it'). The subject of ḏd·f is taken to be the heart, which could bear witness against its owner, as in Spell 30B. It could also be the owner, 'he shall not say what he has done'. Read as irt n·f, the passive participle with n·f, the object would be 'what was done to him'. The sense is doubtful.

sentences.i: It is he who has power over his own limbs.
sentences.n: ntf 'he' is water n, t and the viper f: the independent pronoun. ntf with a participle puts the weight on the subject: 'it is he who has power'. sḫm is written as in line 4 with the owl-and-arm ligature, here without a suffix. m 'over' is the owl, and Budge's line 5 begins with it. ꜥt·f as in line 3. ḏs·f is the cobra ḏ, the bolt s and ·f: ḏs 'self' with a suffix after the noun it stresses, 'his own'.

sentences.i: His heart obeys him.
sentences.n: Budge prints setem-nef as one group, 'hath obeyed him'. It is split here into sḏm, the ear (F21) with m, and n·f 'to him', water n and ·f (q re-indexed): sḏm n 'listen to, obey'. ib·f 'his heart' is the subject, after the verb and its short prepositional phrase. The viper ·f is restored by Budge, printed in brackets. Read as one word, sḏm·n·f, it would be 'his heart has listened', without 'to him'.

sentences.i: He is your lord, and you are in his body.
sentences.n: ntf nb·k 'he is your lord', a sentence without a verb (ntf N 'he is N'). nb·k is the basket nb with the seated man as classifier and ·k: 'you' is now the heart itself. iw·k m ẖt·f, iw with ·k and a prepositional phrase, is a second sentence without a verb, 'you are in his body'. The heart is the servant of the man in whom it lives.

sentences.i: You shall not oppose (him).
sentences.n: nn as before. rq·k is r and the hill-slope q, a cord (coded V1, approximate) and the walking legs as classifiers, and ·k: rq 'oppose, be hostile', as in rqy·k 'your hostility' in Spell 30B, here the sḏm·f after nn, 'you shall not oppose' (Budge: req-k, 'mayest thou not fall away'). The object, the man, is understood.

sentences.i: I am the one who commands that you obey me in the necropolis.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes sḏm with the plinth mꜣꜥ (Aa11) as its complement; read sḏm·k, with the sign m (Aa15). Budge's type gives the sign the closed slanted shape of the plinth in mꜣꜥ-ḫrw, but the ear, ·k and the sense allow only sḏm 'hear, obey'; the plinth keeps its own value in the signs. ink 'I' is the ring in (W24) with k and the seated man. wḏ 'command' is the staff wḏ (coded V24, approximate) with the chick w and the hand d, written twice, as complements, and the roll (Y1): after ink, the participle, 'I am the one who commands'. sḏm·k n·i 'that you obey me' is the sḏm·f after wḏ, saying what is commanded, with n·i 'to me' (water n over the seated man). ẖrt-nṯr as in the title, but here without m 'in', which is not written (Budge supplies '[in]'). The man, not his heart, is master.

sentences.l: the-Osiris · the-scribe · Ani · true-of-voice · in · peace · true-of-voice · in · the-West · beautiful · on · the-place(?) · of · eternity
sentences.i: The Osiris, the scribe Ani, true of voice in peace, true of voice in the beautiful West, on the place(?) of eternity.
sentences.n: wsir is the eye, the seat (Q1) and the seated god, and sš 'scribe' is the palette (Budge: ān); ꜣny has the squatting man with a flail. m ḥtp 'in peace' is the sign m (Aa15) and the offering mat ḥtp with t. The second mꜣꜥ-ḫrw is written out: the sickle mꜣ, the arm ꜥ, the oar ḫrw, the chick w and the man with hand to mouth. imntt 'the West' is the emblem of the West with t twice and the hill-country sign. nfrt 'beautiful' is the heart and windpipe nfr with f, t and r, the t printed before the r: feminine to agree with imntt. ḥr 'on' is the face. The next word is the bolt s (coded O34, approximate) and t with the hill-country sign (N25); Budge reads set, 'the mountain'. It is taken as st 'place', with the classifier of the desert hills where the dead were buried; with an m that is not written, it could be smyt 'desert, necropolis'. nt is the feminine genitive, and ḥḥ is nḥḥ 'eternity', written as in line 2. The spell closes with Ani's name and titles. After this unit Budge prints Spells 29A, 30A and 28 from Naville's edition: other papyri have these spells here, and Ani's papyrus goes on with Spell 58.

sentences.l: spell · of · breathing · air · having-power · over · water · in · the-necropolis
sentences.i: Spell for breathing air and having power over water in the necropolis.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes sst; read ssn. The word is the folded cloth s twice, a small nose (coded D19, approximate) as classifier and t, where Spell 54 has water n; the nose and the air allow no word but ssn 'breathe' (Budge: seset). Spell 58 begins, and Budge's line numerals start again at 1. The papyrus writes rꜣ n ssn nfw sḫm m mw m in red, and ẖrt-nṯr in black. The same writing comes back three times in Spell 59, and the reading is corrected there in the same way. nfw 'air' is the sail (coded P5, approximate) with the chick w and a stroke, as in Spell 54. sḫm 'having power' is the sceptre sḫm with m and the low hooked sign (U15), the classifier of force: an infinitive like ssn, joined to it without 'and'. m mw 'over water': the owl and three lines of water. m ẖrt-nṯr as in Spell 29. Breath and water are what the dead most need, and the spell asks for both.

sentences.l: said · by · the-Osiris · Ani · open · to-me
sentences.i: Said by the Osiris Ani: Open to me!
sentences.n: ḏd in is black here: Budge's red overline ends after the second m. in is the reed and water n. wsir is the low seat (Q2, approximate) over the eye, and ꜣny has the seated man (A1). Budge prints un-nà as one group; it is split here into wn and n·i (q re-indexed). wn 'open' is the hare wn with n, a door-leaf (coded O31) and the low hooked sign as classifiers, as in Spell 26: the imperative, 'open!'. n·i 'to me' is water n over the seated man. Ani stands at a door of the world below and asks to be let through.

sentences.i: Who are you, then?
sentences.n: Budge restores water n with two strokes in brackets, [ni], before the owl and arm. The two groups are joined here into one word, nm 'who?' (q re-indexed): the restored n and strokes (the strokes not read), then the owl m with the arm ꜥ drawn across it in one ligature, the arm not read, as in the Address (Budge: [ni] mā). tr 'then' is t and r with the knotted stalk tr (M6) and the man with hand to mouth: the particle that presses a question. tw (t, w) is the dependent pronoun 'you'. nm tr tw 'who then are you?' is the question that the doorkeepers put in the Address. The door, or its keeper, now speaks.

sentences.i: You are one who travels: where have you come into being(?)?
sentences.n: ntk 'you' (n, t, k) is the independent pronoun, ntk N 'you are N'. sby is the bolt with walking legs under it (O35), which writes sb, with two reeds y: the participle of sbi 'go, pass, travel', 'one who travels' (Budge: sebi, 'journey'). ḫpr·n·k is the scarab ḫpr with r, water n and ·k: the sḏm·n·f, 'you have come into being'. Budge's line numeral 2 is printed inside it, before n·k. The last word is t and water n, then a forked upright (coded O30, approximate), a bird with raised wings (coded G41, approximate) and the roll. It is taken as tnw 'where?', which is written with t and n; the two signs after them are not explained (Budge: ten, 'what?'). The question, and how ntk sby joins it, are uncertain.

sentences.i: I am one of you.
sentences.n: Ani answers. ink 'I' is the ring in (W24) with k and the seated man; no water n is printed above the ring. wꜥ 'one' is the harpoon wꜥ (T21) with a stroke and the arm ꜥ as complement. Budge prints àm and ten as two groups, and they are joined here as im·tn 'of you' (q re-indexed): the reed and the owl, im, the form of m before a suffix, with ·tn. To be one of the gods is the right to pass.

sentences.i: Who is it that is with you?
sentences.n: The keepers ask again. nm 'who?' is water n with the owl-and-arm ligature, here with nothing restored (Budge: nimā). nty 'who is' is water n, t and two strokes y: the relative adjective, used as a noun, 'the one who'. ḥnꜥ·k 'with you' is the wick ḥ, water n and the arm ꜥ, with ·k.

sentences.i: It is Merty.
sentences.n: mrty is the hoe mr (U6) with r, t and two strokes y, then two eyes and the rearing cobra (I12) as classifiers (Budge: Merti). N pw 'it is N' answers the question. The name is written as a dual, and the eyes and the cobra point to a pair of serpent goddesses, the eyes of a god, who go with the dead man; what the name means is not certain.

sentences.l: may-depart-you · from-him · head · from · head · in · entering · the-Meseqet
sentences.i: Part from him, head from head, on entering the Meseqet.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes msqn; read msqt. The last word is the three skins ms (F31) with s as complement, the hill-slope q, water n where t is expected, the house and the seated god (coded A40, approximate). It is the Meseqet of Spell 17, which is written with t, and no word msqn is known (Budge: Mesqen). rwi·k is r, the chick w, the reed i, the walking legs (a small Λ) and ·k: rwi 'go away, depart from', the sḏm·f used as a command, 'may you depart' (Budge: ruà-k, 'separate thou'). r·f 'from him' is r with ·f. tp m-ꜥ tp 'head from head': the head with its stroke twice, with the owl and the arm set high beside it, m-ꜥ 'from'. Budge's numeral 3 stands before tkn. m tkn 'on entering' is the sign m (Aa15) with tkn 'approach, enter', t, k, n and the walking legs: the infinitive. Who speaks, and to whom, is not said: perhaps the keepers send Merty away from the dead man at the Meseqet. The Meseqet is a place in the world below that the dead pass through.

sentences.i: He lets me cross to the mansion of those who find faces.
sentences.n: di·f is the giving hand with its loaf (D37) and ·f: rdi 'let', without its r, in the sḏm·f, 'he lets'. Who 'he' is, is not said. ḏꜣ·i is the fire-drill ḏꜣ (coded U28, approximate) with ꜣ, a boat (coded P1, approximate) as classifier and ·i: ḏꜣi 'cross (water)', the sḏm·f after rdi, 'he lets me cross' (Budge: t'a-à, 'that I may travel'). r 'to'. ḥwt 'mansion, temple' is the enclosure ḥwt (O6) with t and the house, and nt is the feminine genitive. gm-ḥrw is the ibis gm (G28) with m, then the face with its stroke, a second stroke and the seated god: gm 'find' with ḥrw 'faces', the plural written with the strokes, and the god sign classifying the whole as divine beings. It is taken as a participle phrase used as a name, 'those who find faces' (Budge prints it as one group, qem-ḥràu, and supplies 'the gods' and 'their'). What finding faces means is not clear.

sentences.i: 'Gatherer of Bas' is the name of my ferry-boat.
sentences.n: From here the dead man names the parts of his boat: to know their names is to be able to cross in it. sꜣq is the folded cloth s, a box-like sign (coded Aa18, approximate), which writes sꜣ, ꜣ and the hill-slope q, with a fist-like sign (coded D49, approximate) and the roll as classifiers: sꜣq 'gather', the participle, as in Spell 147 (Budge: saq, 'assembler'). bꜣw 'bas, souls' is the jabiru bꜣ (G29) with the small bowl (R7) at its foot, not read, and two strokes for the plural; Budge's type prints the first stroke short and high. sꜣq bꜣw, a participle and its object, is the name 'Gatherer of Bas'. Budge's line numeral 4 stands before rn. rn n 'the name of' is the mouth r, water n and the man with hand to mouth, then the genitive n. N rn n X, a name before rn, is a sentence without a verb, 'N is the name of X'. mḫnt·i 'my ferry-boat' is the owl and arm in one ligature, read m with the arm, as in the Address, then the belly (F32) standing for ḫ, water n, t, two strokes (not read) and a boat (coded P1, approximate) as classifier, with ·i (Budge: māχenti).

sentences.i: 'Hair-Raging(?)' is the name of the oars.
sentences.n: nšy is water n and the pool š (coded N37, approximate) with two reeds y, a lock of hair (D3, approximate) and the low hooked sign as classifiers. It is taken as nšny 'storm, rage', its second n not written; the hair and the classifier of force suggest hair bristling with rage (Budge: neśi, 'making to stand'). šny 'hair' is the cord šn (coded V7, approximate) with n, two strokes y, the lock of hair and a stroke. The name is doubtful. wsrw 'oars' is the head and neck of a jackal wsr (F12) with s and r as complements, the chick w and a branch-like sign (coded M3, approximate), the classifier of wood, with plural strokes (Budge: useru). It is a second word of the spelling wsr 'strong', the oar of a boat.

sentences.i: 'Goad(?)' is the name of the hold(?).
sentences.n: srt is the folded cloth s, r and t with a thorn (coded M44, approximate) and the branch (M3, approximate) as classifiers: a pointed thing of wood, a goad or thorn (Budge: sert, 'goad'). rn n as before, with the seated man (A1) after rn. mḏꜣbt is the owl drawn with the arm across it, the fire-drill ḏꜣ (coded U28, approximate) with ꜣ, b and t, and the branch as classifier. Budge's numeral 5 is printed inside the word, after the owl. He reads mat'abet, without the arm, and renders it 'the hold'. The word is not known otherwise, and the wood classifier says only that it is a part of the boat.

sentences.i: '(Smt?) Straight' is the name of the rudder.
sentences.n: smt is the bolt s, a flat sign with one end turned down and a small loop at the other (coded D53, approximate, as mt), t, two tall strokes (coded Z4A) and the roll. The second sign is not identified, and the word is not known and is left untranslated; Budge reads semet and renders 'making straight for'. ꜥqꜣ is the arm ꜥ, the hill-slope q and the vulture ꜣ, with the same two strokes and the roll: ꜥqꜣ 'straight, exact', the word for a true course or a plumb-line (Budge: āqa, 'the middle'). rn n as before, with the man with hand to mouth. ḥmy 'the rudder' is the well ḥm (coded N41, approximate) with m, two reeds y, the steering-oar (coded P10, approximate) and the branch: ḥmw 'steering-oar', its ending written here with y. Steering straight is the rudder's work, and ꜥqꜣ seems to say so; what smt adds is not known.

sentences.i: Likewise (stwt?): you bury yourself(?) in the pool(?).
sentences.n: Budge's English for the second and third words is only a row of dots, and the passage is not understood. mitt 'likewise, the like' is the milk-jug in its net (coded W19, approximate), which writes mi, with t twice and the roll (Budge: màtet). stwt is the folded cloth s, t, the chick w and t, with a standing mummy-shaped figure (coded A53, approximate), the classifier of images and statues. The stwt 'rays' of the published parts is spelt the same, but light does not take this classifier, and the word here is not known; twt 'image' may be in it, but that is a guess, and it is left untranslated. Budge prints qeres-k-tu as one group, split here into qrs·k and tw (q re-indexed). qrs·k is the hill-slope q, r and the bolt s with the low hooked sign (U15) and ·k: qrs 'bury', the sḏm·f, 'you bury'. What the low sign classifies here, perhaps a coffin on its sledge, is not clear. tw (t, w) is the dependent pronoun 'you', the object: 'yourself'. Budge's numeral 6 stands before m 'in'. The next word is the bolt s, the hare wn with n, three lines of water, a pool (coded N37, approximate) and a small wedge (coded N21, approximate) with a stroke. It is taken as the name of some water, swn (Budge: sun, 'the lake'), not known otherwise. A mouth r follows with no English in Budge and is not translated.

sentences.l: may-give-you · to-me · a-jug · of · milk · a-cake · a-loaf(?) · a-portion(?) · a-great-(amount) · of · meat · in · the-mansion · of · Anubis
sentences.i: May you give me a jug of milk, a cake, a loaf(?), a portion(?) and plenty of meat in the mansion of Anubis.
sentences.n: Budge prints erṭāi-ten-nà as one group; it is split here into rdy·tn and n·i (q re-indexed). rdy·tn is the mouth r, the arm (D36, no loaf), two reeds y and ·tn: rdi 'give', its weak y written, in the sḏm·f used as a wish, 'may you give'. The 'you' is plural, the gods of the mansion. mhr 'jug' is the owl with the arm, read m as in mḫnt, the courtyard h, r, the reed and a small lidded pot with lugs (coded W22, approximate) as classifier (Budge: māḥerà); the reed is not explained. n irtt 'of milk': irtt is the reed, the eye ir, t twice and two milk-jugs in a net (coded W20, approximate) with a stroke. šns 'cake' is the cord šn (V7, approximate) with n, the bolt s and a long loaf (coded X4, approximate), as in the rubric of Spell 125. The next word is the house (O1), the bolt s, two strokes and a loaf (X4, approximate). Budge reads pasi, 'loaves', as if the first sign were the stool p; in the type it is the house, which writes pr. It is taken, by its loaf, as a kind of bread, psy, not known otherwise; the reading is doubtful. dni is the hand d, water n and two strokes y with the lugged pot: dni 'portion, share', here a measure of drink by its pot (Budge prints ṭeni (sic), 'cups of drink'). wr n iwf 'plenty of meat': wr, the swallow with r, used as a noun, 'a great amount', the genitive n, and iwf 'meat', the reed, the chick w and f, with a piece of flesh (coded F51, approximate) and plural strokes. Budge's numeral 7 is printed inside iwf, before the flesh, and his line 7 begins with the m after it. m ḥwt nt inpw 'in the mansion of Anubis': ḥwt as in line 3, and inpw 'Anubis', the reed, n, p and w, with the jackal-headed god (C6). Anubis, the god of embalming, watched over the offerings at the tomb.

sentences.l: if · is-known · spell · this · (iw)-he · enters-he · after · coming-forth · from · the-necropolis · (nt)
sentences.i: If this spell is known, he will go in after coming forth from the necropolis.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes ir rḫ rꜣ pn iw·f ꜥq·f m-ḫt prt m in red; ẖrt-nṯr and the last word are black. This is the rubric of Spell 58, the note on its use that follows the spell. ir 'if' is the reed and r. rḫ 'is known' is r and ḫ with the roll: the passive sḏm·f, without an ending. rꜣ pn 'this spell'. iw·f ꜥq·f 'he will go in' is iw with ·f, then the cormorant ꜥq (coded G35, approximate) with q and the walking legs, and ·f: iw·f sḏm·f, a statement of what will happen. m-ḫt 'after' is the owl and the branch ḫt (M3) with ḫ and t as complements and the walking legs: the compound preposition. prt 'coming forth' is the house pr with r, the walking legs and t: the infinitive of pri. m ẖrt-nṯr is written out here: the flag, the block ẖr over r, t and the hill-country sign (coded N25, approximate). A last nt, water n and t, has no English in Budge; it is not translated, and it may begin a phrase that was not finished. To go out and come back in again is the freedom of the dead, and the rubric promises it.

sentences.l: spell · of · breathing · air · having-power · over · water · in · the-necropolis
sentences.i: Spell for breathing air and having power over water in the necropolis.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes sst; read ssn, as in Spell 58. Spell 59 begins, and Budge's line numerals start again at 1. The papyrus writes rꜣ n ssn nfw sḫm m mw m in red, and ẖrt-nṯr in black. The title is that of Spell 58. Here the t stands above the nose; the nose and the air allow only ssn 'breathe'. The spell asks the same things, but of the sycamore of the sky-goddess Nut.

sentences.l: said · by · the-Osiris · Ani · O · sycamore · this · of · Nut
sentences.i: Said by the Osiris Ani: O this sycamore of Nut!
sentences.n: The papyrus writes ḏd in in red; here the overline covers only those two words. in is the reed and water n, and ꜣny has the seated man (A1). i 'O' is the reed with the man with hand to mouth. nht 'sycamore' is water n, the courtyard h and t, with a tree (M1) as classifier, and a curved stick (coded M3, approximate), the classifier of wood, laid across its crown (Budge: nehet). twy 'this' is t, the chick w and two reeds y: the feminine demonstrative, agreeing with nht. nt is the feminine genitive. nwt 'Nut' is the pot nw with t and the sky (N1). In the tombs of this time the goddess is shown in a sycamore, pouring water for the dead and handing them bread.

sentences.i: May you give me some of the water and air that are in you.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes n; read mw. Only one line of water is printed, and Budge queries his mu; the titles have mw 'water', and the sense needs it. Budge prints ṭāt-nà as one group; it is split here into di·t and n·i (q re-indexed). di·t is the giving hand with its loaf (D37) and t, the suffix ·t 'you', feminine, for the sycamore: rdi without its r, in the sḏm·f used as a wish, 'may you give'. m is the owl: m of a part, 'some of'. Budge's numeral 2 stands before nfw 'air', and no word for 'and' is written. im·t 'in you' is the reed, the owl and the crossed planks im (Z11): im written out before its sign, the form of m before a suffix, with t, the feminine suffix (Budge: àmt). The tree of the sky-goddess is asked to share what it holds.

sentences.i: I am the one who embraces this seat in the midst of Wenu (Hermopolis).
sentences.n: ink 'I' as before. sḫn is the bolt s, ḫ and n with two embracing arms (coded D32, approximate) as classifier: sḫn 'embrace', the participle after ink, 'I am the one who embraces' (Budge: seχen). st 'seat' is the seat (coded Q1, approximate) with t and the house. twy 'this', as in line 1. ḥryt-ib is the face ḥr with its stroke and the heart ib, with t: the nisba ḥry-ib 'which is in the midst of', feminine to agree with st, its t written after the heart. wnw is the hare wn with n, the chick w and the town sign: Wenu, the city of Thoth in Middle Egypt, called Hermopolis by the Greeks (Budge: Unnu); the published parts also call it Khemenu. Wenu was said to be the place where the world began, and the egg of the next line belongs to that beginning.

sentences.i: I have guarded this egg of the Great Cackler.
sentences.n: iw opens the statement and is not translated. sꜣw·n·i is the herdsman with his stick (A47), the sign of sꜣw 'guard', with ꜣ and w as complements, the low hooked sign (U15) as classifier, water n and ·i: the sḏm·n·f, 'I have guarded', as in Spell 54. Budge's numeral 3 stands before swḥt 'egg', the folded cloth s, the chick w, the wick ḥ, t and the egg. twy 'this' and nt 'of' as in line 1. ngg-wr 'the Great Cackler' is water n with the jar-stand g twice and the goose (G38), then the swallow wr with r and the seated god. Budge prints two groups, neḳeḳ and ur, and they are joined here as one name, as in Spell 54 (q re-indexed); here the goose is the classifier of ngg, and wr has its own bird. The Great Cackler is the goose of the beginning of things, whose egg held the first life.

sentences.i: It grows, and I grow; it lives, and I live.
sentences.n: rd·s is the mouth r and the hand d with the bowstring sign (coded T12, approximate), which writes rd, and the folded cloth s as ·s 'it', feminine for the egg: rd 'grow', the sḏm·f (Budge: ruṭ-s). rd·i 'I grow' has the reed and the man with hand to mouth for ·i. ꜥnḫ·s 'it lives' is the sign ꜥnḫ with n and ḫ as complements and the bolt as ·s, and ꜥnḫ·i 'I live' has the seated man. As in Spell 54, the dead man's life is bound to the life of the egg.

sentences.l: breathes-it · air · breathe-I · air · the-Osiris · Ani · in · vindication
sentences.i: It breathes air, and I breathe air, I, the Osiris Ani, in vindication.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes sst·s and sst·i; read ssn·s and ssn·i, as in the title. Budge's numeral 4 stands before ssn·s. ssn·s 'it breathes' has the folded cloth s as ·s, and ssn·i 'I breathe' the seated man. nfw 'air' twice, as before. wsir ꜣny 'the Osiris Ani' stands after the verbs as a name in apposition to 'I' (Budge supplies '[I]'); ꜣny has the squatting man with a flail. m mꜣꜥ-ḫrw is the sign m (Aa15) with mꜣꜥ-ḫrw used as a noun, 'in vindication': the plinth and the oar, without the sickle. The spell ends as Spell 54 does, with the dead man breathing.
